nodes.label: IPv6
nodes.description: Internet Protocol version 6; the most recent IP version described by the source, providing identification/location and routing across interconnected IP networks.

nodes.label: Internet Protocol
nodes.description: Network-layer internetworking protocol family providing packet-switched datagram delivery.

nodes.label: IPv4
nodes.description: 32-bit predecessor IP protocol whose address exhaustion motivated IPv6.

nodes.label: Internet Engineering Task Force
nodes.description: Standards organization that developed and standardized IPv6.

nodes.label: Internet Layer
nodes.description: Internet Protocol suite layer occupied by IPv4 and IPv6.

nodes.label: OSI Network Layer
nodes.description: OSI layer associated with IPv6.

nodes.label: Packet-switched internetworking
nodes.description: IPv6 provides end-to-end datagram transmission across multiple IP networks.

nodes.label: IP datagram
nodes.description: End-to-end network-layer data unit carried across multiple IP networks.

nodes.label: End-to-end principle
nodes.description: Design principle emphasizing processing and integrity responsibilities at endpoints rather than requiring extensive intermediate-node processing.

nodes.label: IPv6 128-bit address space
nodes.description: 2^128 possible address values, approximately 3.4×10^38.

nodes.label: Hierarchical route aggregation
nodes.description: Hierarchical IPv6 allocation facilitates route aggregation and can limit routing-table expansion.

nodes.label: IPv6 multicast
nodes.description: Base IPv6 transmission mode allowing one packet send to multiple destinations.

nodes.label: IPv6 unicast
nodes.description: One-to-one IPv6 transmission mode.

nodes.label: IPv6 anycast
nodes.description: IPv6 transmission mode selecting an appropriate member of an anycast group.

nodes.label: IPv4 broadcast
nodes.description: Traditional one-to-all attached-link addressing mode absent from IPv6.

nodes.label: No IPv6 broadcast
nodes.description: IPv6 has no broadcast address; all-nodes multicast is used for the analogous attached-link function.

nodes.label: IPv4 32-bit address space
nodes.description: IPv4 provides 2^32, approximately 4.3 billion, addresses.

nodes.label: Internet commercialization and growth
nodes.description: Rapid Internet growth after commercialization made the IPv4 address supply problem apparent.

nodes.label: Classless Inter-Domain Routing
nodes.description: Classless addressing redesign used to improve IPv4 address-space efficiency but insufficient to prevent exhaustion.

nodes.label: IANA
nodes.description: Internet Assigned Numbers Authority, which allocated the last unassigned top-level IPv4 blocks to RIRs in February 2011.

nodes.label: Regional Internet Registries
nodes.description: Regional registries receiving IPv4 blocks and distributing address space to subordinate registries/LIRs.

nodes.label: APNIC
nodes.description: Asia-Pacific Network Information Centre.

nodes.label: RIPE NCC
nodes.description: Regional Internet Registry that reported exhaustion of its IPv4 address pool on 25 November 2019.

nodes.label: LACNIC
nodes.description: Latin America and Caribbean regional Internet registry.

nodes.label: AFRINIC
nodes.description: African regional Internet registry.

nodes.label: ARIN
nodes.description: American Registry for Internet Numbers.

nodes.label: IPv6 address
nodes.description: 128-bit network-layer identifier represented as eight 16-bit hexadecimal groups.

nodes.label: 16-bit hexadecimal group
nodes.description: One of eight 16-bit groups in textual IPv6 notation.

nodes.label: Colon separator
nodes.description: Separates hexadecimal address groups.

nodes.label: Leading-zero suppression
nodes.description: Leading zeros in individual hexadecimal groups may be omitted.

nodes.label: Double-colon compression
nodes.description: One consecutive run of zero groups may be replaced with :: exactly once.
IPv6 loopback address.

nodes.label: Bracketed IPv6 URL host
nodes.description: IPv6 literals used as URL hosts are enclosed in square brackets so colons are not confused with the port separator.

nodes.label: IPv6 routing prefix
nodes.description: Most-significant 64 bits of the common IPv6 subnet structure.

nodes.label: 64-bit interface identifier
nodes.description: Lower 64 bits used as the interface identifier in the source's general IPv6 subnet model.

nodes.label: IPv6 packet
nodes.description: IPv6 packet consisting of a fixed base header followed by optional extension headers and payload.

nodes.label: IPv6 fixed header
nodes.description: Fixed 40-octet base header containing core forwarding and delivery fields.

nodes.label: 40-octet base header
nodes.description: Minimum/fixed IPv6 base header size: 320 bits.

nodes.label: Source Address
nodes.description: 128-bit source address in the IPv6 base header.

nodes.label: Destination Address
nodes.description: 128-bit destination address in the IPv6 base header.

nodes.label: Traffic Class
nodes.description: IPv6 traffic-class field used for differentiated services and explicit congestion notification.

nodes.label: DSCP
nodes.description: 6-bit Differentiated Services Code Point component of Traffic Class.

nodes.label: ECN
nodes.description: 2-bit Explicit Congestion Notification component of Traffic Class.

nodes.label: Hop Limit
nodes.description: IPv6 hop-count field replacing IPv4 TTL semantics.

nodes.label: Next Header
nodes.description: Identifies the next extension header or upper-layer protocol.

nodes.label: IPv6 payload
nodes.description: Data following the base header and any extension-header chain.

nodes.label: IPv6 extension headers
nodes.description: Optional headers carrying special-purpose functions such as routing, fragmentation and IPsec.

nodes.label: Routing extension header
nodes.description: IPv6 extension header used for routing-related special treatment.

nodes.label: Fragment extension header
nodes.description: Extension header enabling endpoint fragmentation.

nodes.label: Hop-by-Hop Options header
nodes.description: Extension header associated with options requiring special treatment along the path, including the Jumbo Payload option.

nodes.label: IPsec Authentication Header
nodes.description: IPsec AH implemented as an IPv6 extension header.

nodes.label: IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload
nodes.description: IPsec ESP implemented as an IPv6 extension header.

nodes.label: IPv6 jumbogram
nodes.description: IPv6 packet with payload beyond the ordinary 64-KB limit, up to 2^32−1 octets under the Jumbo Payload option.

nodes.label: Jumbo Payload Option
nodes.description: Hop-by-Hop option indicating a jumbo payload.

nodes.label: 1280-octet IPv6 minimum/default MTU
nodes.description: Source states hosts must keep packets within a default maximum transmission unit of 1280 octets when not otherwise using PMTU discovery/fragmentation.

nodes.label: IPv6 router
nodes.description: Router forwarding IPv6 packets across networks.

nodes.label: IPv6 router packet processing
nodes.description: Forwarding benefits from a simpler base header, aligned fields and moving uncommon options into extension headers, while software implementations and extension headers can degrade performance.

nodes.label: IPv4 header checksum
nodes.description: IPv4 header integrity checksum recalculated when TTL changes.

nodes.label: No IPv6 base-header checksum
nodes.description: IPv6 removes the base-header checksum.

nodes.label: TCP
nodes.description: Transport protocol providing higher-layer integrity/reliability functions cited by the source.

nodes.label: UDP
nodes.description: Transport protocol whose checksum is mandatory in IPv6.

nodes.label: Path MTU Discovery
nodes.description: Mechanism hosts use to determine a packet size that can traverse the path without router fragmentation.

nodes.label: Endpoint fragmentation
nodes.description: IPv6 fragmentation is performed by hosts using the Fragment extension header.

nodes.label: No router fragmentation
nodes.description: IPv6 routers do not perform IP fragmentation.

nodes.label: Software IPv6 forwarding
nodes.description: Some devices implement IPv6 support in software rather than hardware, potentially causing poor packet-processing performance.

nodes.label: Extension-header CPU processing
nodes.description: Extension headers can cause router CPU processing and performance/security problems in some implementations.

nodes.label: IPv6 link-local unicast
nodes.description: Required interface-local IPv6 address using fe80::/10.

nodes.label: fe80::/10
nodes.description: Prefix used by IPv6 link-local unicast addresses.

nodes.label: IPv6 global unicast
nodes.description: Globally unique IPv6 address type used for routable addressing.

nodes.label: IPv6 temporary/privacy address
nodes.description: Random, unstable SLAAC-derived address intended to reduce tracking exposure.

nodes.label: SLAAC
nodes.description: Stateless Address Autoconfiguration; hosts generate link-local addresses and configure network prefixes using router advertisements.

nodes.label: DHCPv6
nodes.description: Stateful IPv6 configuration mechanism that can supply additional addresses or other configuration.

nodes.label: Router Advertisement
nodes.description: ICMPv6 message carrying IPv6 network configuration information and prefix data.

nodes.label: Router Solicitation
nodes.description: ICMPv6 message sent by a host to the all-routers multicast group to discover IPv6 routers.

nodes.label: ICMPv6
nodes.description: ICMP version associated with IPv6, including router discovery and neighbor discovery.

nodes.label: Neighbor Discovery Protocol
nodes.description: IPv6 mechanism for mapping IP addresses to link-layer addresses and discovering routers, using ICMPv6 and multicast.

nodes.label: Neighbor Solicitation
nodes.description: NDP message used in address uniqueness checking and neighbor/link-layer resolution.

nodes.label: ff02::2 all-routers multicast
nodes.description: All-routers multicast group used by IPv6 hosts for router solicitation.

nodes.label: ff02::1 all-nodes multicast
nodes.description: All-nodes link-local multicast group providing the broadcast-like all-host function.

nodes.label: Duplicate Address Detection
nodes.description: Local-link uniqueness checking for IPv6 addresses using neighbor solicitation.

nodes.label: On-link flag
nodes.description: Router Advertisement flag telling the host to treat subnet addresses as directly on-link for the stated lifetime.

nodes.label: Manage flag
nodes.description: Router Advertisement flag indicating whether DHCP should supply additional addresses.

nodes.label: Other flag
nodes.description: Router Advertisement flag indicating whether additional configuration information should be obtained via DHCP.

nodes.label: Prefix Information option
nodes.description: Router Advertisement information carrying subnet prefixes, lifetimes and flags.

nodes.label: Address flag
nodes.description: Flag telling a host to create a global address from the advertised prefix.

nodes.label: Router Renumbering
nodes.description: Protocol for stateless router/network renumbering discussed in the source.

nodes.label: RFC 7217 interface identifiers
nodes.description: Hash-based method recommended for stable, semantically opaque IPv6 interface identifiers.

nodes.label: MAC-derived interface identifier
nodes.description: Earlier link-local interface identifier method derived from the network-interface MAC address.

nodes.label: IPv6 address privacy
nodes.description: Privacy concern arising from stable globally addressable identifiers and mitigated by temporary addresses.

nodes.label: Domain Name System
nodes.description: Naming system used to map hostnames to IPv6 addresses and support dual-stack address discovery.

nodes.label: AAAA record
nodes.description: DNS resource record mapping a hostname to an IPv6 address.

nodes.label: A record
nodes.description: DNS resource record mapping a hostname to an IPv4 address.

nodes.label: ip6.arpa
nodes.description: Reverse-DNS namespace for IPv6, hierarchically represented using hexadecimal nibbles.

nodes.label: A6 record
nodes.description: Historical IPv6 DNS record type associated with renumbering; later deprecated to experimental status.

nodes.label: Dual-stack DNS resolution
nodes.description: A dual-stack client queries for AAAA and A records and selects an address according to routing and address-selection policy.

nodes.label: IPv6 default address selection
nodes.description: Policy used to choose between available IPv6 and IPv4 destinations.

nodes.label: Happy Eyeballs
nodes.description: Dual-stack connection strategy designed to use IPv6 when available while preserving connectivity via IPv4.

nodes.label: IPv6 transition
nodes.description: Collection of mechanisms allowing IPv4 and IPv6 to coexist while IPv6 deployment proceeds.

nodes.label: Dual-stack
nodes.description: Complete IPv4 and IPv6 protocol stacks operating simultaneously over common lower-layer infrastructure.

nodes.label: IPv6 tunneling
nodes.description: Encapsulation of IPv6 packets within IPv4 infrastructure or vice versa.

nodes.label: 6to4
nodes.description: Historical tunneling mechanism carrying IPv6 over IPv4 infrastructure.

nodes.label: Teredo
nodes.description: IPv6-over-IPv4 mechanism encapsulating IPv6 packets in UDP.

nodes.label: Teredo relay
nodes.description: IPv6 router mediating between a Teredo server and native IPv6 network.

nodes.label: NAT64
nodes.description: IPv4/IPv6 translation mechanism allowing IPv6-facing addressing to reach IPv4 services; source also describes IPv4 LAN translation into a public IPv6 address.

nodes.label: IPv4-mapped IPv6 address
nodes.description: IPv6 representation of an IPv4 address using a 96-bit prefix and embedded 32-bit IPv4 value.

nodes.label: IPv4-compatible IPv6 address
nodes.description: Deprecated earlier hybrid address form.

nodes.label: 64:ff9b::/96
nodes.description: IPv4-embedded IPv6 prefix used for NAT64 methods.

nodes.label: Tunnel MTU reduction
nodes.description: Encapsulation reduces available MTU and complicates Path MTU Discovery.

nodes.label: IPv4-only service
nodes.description: Service reachable only through IPv4 addressing/protocol stack.

nodes.label: IPsec
nodes.description: Internet Protocol Security framework associated with IPv6 security.

nodes.label: IKEv2
nodes.description: Key-management protocol required by IPv6 IPsec implementations under the source's cited requirements.

nodes.label: IPv6 IPsec minimum algorithms
nodes.description: Minimum cryptographic algorithm support required for interoperable IPsec implementations.

nodes.label: IPv6 shadow network
nodes.description: Unmanaged IPv6 connectivity that can bypass IPv4-only security management.

nodes.label: IPv4-only security controls
nodes.description: Security infrastructure that may fail to inspect IPv6 traffic if IPv6 is enabled without corresponding controls.

nodes.label: IPv6 fragmentation evasion
nodes.description: Fragmentation can be used to evade network security controls.

nodes.label: RA-Guard
nodes.description: Control for IPv6 Router Advertisement attacks/evasion; source discusses fragmentation-related evasion.

nodes.label: Secure Neighbor Discovery
nodes.description: Security mechanism associated with protecting Neighbor Discovery.

nodes.label: IPv6 implementation security
nodes.description: Security depends both on IPv6 protocol properties and implementation correctness.

nodes.label: IPv6 mobility
nodes.description: IPv6 mobility design includes Mobile IPv6 and support for moving subnets.

nodes.label: Mobile IPv6
nodes.description: Mobile IPv6 avoids triangular routing relative to mobile IPv4 according to the source.

nodes.label: Subnet mobility
nodes.description: IPv6 routers may allow entire subnets to move to a new connection point without renumbering.

nodes.description: IETF began developing a next-generation IP protocol in response to projected Internet growth.

nodes.label: 1993 IPng area
nodes.description: IETF created a temporary ad hoc IP Next Generation area in September 1993.

nodes.label: 1994 IPng model adoption
nodes.description: IETF adopted the IPng model on 25 July 1994.

nodes.description: First RFC standardizing IPv6, released in 1995.

nodes.label: RFC 2460
nodes.description: 1998 IPv6 specification that was later superseded by RFC 8200.

nodes.label: RFC 8200
nodes.description: 2017 Internet Standard for IPv6, superseding RFC 2460.

nodes.label: RFC 8201
nodes.description: IPv6 Path MTU Discovery standard related to finding efficient path packet size.

nodes.label: 1998 IPv6 Draft Standard
nodes.description: IPv6 became an IETF Draft Standard in December 1998.

nodes.label: 2017 IPv6 Internet Standard
nodes.description: IPv6 was ratified as an Internet Standard on 14 July 2017.

nodes.label: 1999 IPv6 deployment beginning
nodes.description: Source identifies July 1999 as the beginning of IPv6 deployment.

nodes.label: Beijing 2008 IPv6 deployment
nodes.description: IPv6 was used in a major world event at the Beijing 2008 Olympics.

nodes.label: 2011 production OS support
nodes.description: By 2011 major personal-computer and server operating systems had production-quality IPv6 implementations.

nodes.label: Autonomous System

nodes.label: BGP
nodes.description: Inter-domain routing protocol used for IPv4/IPv6 prefix advertisement and deployment measurement.

nodes.label: Internet Service Provider
nodes.description: Provider that may assign IPv6 prefixes/addresses and provide IPv4/IPv6 connectivity.

nodes.label: Regional Internet Registries
nodes.description: Regional bodies participating in IPv6/IPv4 address allocation.

nodes.description: Number of possible 128-bit IPv6 address values; approximately 3.4×10^38.

nodes.description: General subnet structure presented by the source.

nodes.description: IPv6 link-local unicast prefix.

nodes.description: Link-local all-nodes multicast group used for the broadcast-like function.

nodes.description: Multicast destination used for Router Solicitation.

nodes.label: NAT64 IPv4-embedded prefix
nodes.description: IPv4-embedded IPv6 prefix for NAT64.

nodes.label: IPv6 loopback
nodes.description: Loopback address.

nodes.description: Maximum payload size stated for jumbograms.

nodes.description: Payload must be below 64 KB without Jumbo Payload option.

nodes.description: Default maximum transmission unit cited in the host fragmentation discussion.

nodes.label: IPv6 vs IPv4
nodes.description: IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses and a different packet/header model; IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses and its own packet format.

nodes.label: Unicast vs anycast vs multicast
nodes.description: IPv6 defines all three transmission/addressing modes with different destination semantics.

nodes.label: Multicast vs broadcast
nodes.description: IPv6 has no broadcast; all-nodes multicast supplies the analogous attached-link all-host function.

nodes.label: SLAAC vs DHCPv6
nodes.description: SLAAC is stateless host/router-based prefix configuration; DHCPv6 can supply additional stateful addresses or information.

nodes.label: Link-local vs global unicast
nodes.description: Link-local addresses are local-link and required on IPv6 interfaces; global unicast addresses are globally routable.

nodes.label: Base header vs extension headers
nodes.description: The base header is fixed at 40 octets; optional functions are moved to extension headers.

nodes.label: Router fragmentation vs endpoint fragmentation
nodes.description: IPv6 routers do not fragment; endpoints can fragment and hosts can use PMTU discovery.

nodes.label: IPv6 no header checksum vs IPv4 checksum
nodes.description: IPv6 omits the base-header checksum, unlike IPv4, reducing router recalculation work.

nodes.label: Dual-stack vs tunneling
nodes.description: Dual-stack runs both stacks natively; tunneling encapsulates one protocol within another network.

nodes.label: IPv4-mapped vs IPv4-compatible
nodes.description: IPv4-mapped addresses remain a hybrid representation; IPv4-compatible addresses are deprecated.

nodes.label: Stable vs temporary addresses
nodes.description: Stable/global identifiers support reachability but can facilitate tracking; temporary addresses reduce persistence.

nodes.label: AAAA vs A DNS records
nodes.description: AAAA resolves IPv6; A resolves IPv4.

nodes.label: PMTU discovery vs fragmentation
nodes.description: PMTU discovery sizes packets for the path; fragmentation is endpoint-only when needed.

nodes.label: IPsec vs higher-layer security
nodes.description: The source discusses IPsec at the IP layer but does not equate it with TLS; both occupy different architectural positions.

nodes.label: Native vs tunneled IPv6
nodes.description: Native IPv6 traverses IPv6-capable infrastructure; tunneling carries IPv6 over IPv4 infrastructure.

nodes.label: IPv6 is just IPv4 with bigger addresses
nodes.description: IPv6 changes packet format, address architecture, fragmentation behavior, neighbor discovery, multicast/broadcast semantics and other protocol functions.

nodes.label: IPv6 supports broadcast
nodes.description: IPv6 does not define traditional broadcast addresses; multicast is used instead.

nodes.label: Routers fragment IPv6 packets
nodes.description: IPv6 routers do not fragment; hosts use PMTU discovery or endpoint fragmentation.

nodes.label: IPv6 addresses always need DHCP
nodes.description: IPv6 supports SLAAC and hosts generate link-local addresses automatically; DHCPv6 is optional for additional state.

nodes.label: Every IPv6 address is globally routable
nodes.description: IPv6 interfaces require link-local addressing and may have multiple address types; global unicast is only one category.

nodes.label: IPv6 cannot be scanned
nodes.description: The source explicitly notes that configuration patterns can make scanning feasible in real-world scenarios.

nodes.label: IPv6 has a header checksum like IPv4
nodes.description: IPv6 omits the base-header checksum.

nodes.label: IPv6 and IPv4 interoperate directly
nodes.description: The source states the protocols are not directly interoperable and require transition mechanisms.

nodes.label: IPv6 extension headers are always harmless to routers
nodes.description: Some implementations process extension headers in software/CPU paths, causing performance or security issues.

nodes.label: Global IPv6 addressing eliminates privacy concerns
nodes.description: Stable globally addressable identifiers can facilitate tracking; temporary addresses mitigate this concern.

nodes.label: Tunneling is equivalent to native IPv6
nodes.description: Tunneling adds encapsulation and can reduce MTU/increase latency.

nodes.label: NDP is just ARP with a new address format
nodes.description: NDP uses ICMPv6 and multicast and also handles router discovery and address configuration.

nodes.label: AAAA records are IPv4 DNS records
nodes.description: AAAA records map names to IPv6 addresses; A records map names to IPv4.

nodes.label: IPv6 deployment means IPv4 disappears immediately
nodes.description: The source describes coexistence and transition mechanisms because both protocols operate simultaneously.

nodes.label: IPv6 security is automatically stronger because of the larger address space
nodes.description: The source identifies implementation and operational security risks, including shadow networks and fragmentation evasion.

semantic_distinctions.label: No IPv6 broadcast
semantic_distinctions.description: IPv6 has no broadcast address; all-nodes multicast is used for the analogous attached-link function.

semantic_distinctions.label: IPv6 vs IPv4
semantic_distinctions.description: IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses and a different packet/header model; IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses and its own packet format.

semantic_distinctions.label: Unicast vs anycast vs multicast
semantic_distinctions.description: IPv6 defines all three transmission/addressing modes with different destination semantics.

semantic_distinctions.label: Multicast vs broadcast
semantic_distinctions.description: IPv6 has no broadcast; all-nodes multicast supplies the analogous attached-link all-host function.

semantic_distinctions.label: SLAAC vs DHCPv6
semantic_distinctions.description: SLAAC is stateless host/router-based prefix configuration; DHCPv6 can supply additional stateful addresses or information.

semantic_distinctions.label: Link-local vs global unicast
semantic_distinctions.description: Link-local addresses are local-link and required on IPv6 interfaces; global unicast addresses are globally routable.

semantic_distinctions.label: Base header vs extension headers
semantic_distinctions.description: The base header is fixed at 40 octets; optional functions are moved to extension headers.

semantic_distinctions.label: Router fragmentation vs endpoint fragmentation
semantic_distinctions.description: IPv6 routers do not fragment; endpoints can fragment and hosts can use PMTU discovery.

semantic_distinctions.label: IPv6 no header checksum vs IPv4 checksum
semantic_distinctions.description: IPv6 omits the base-header checksum, unlike IPv4, reducing router recalculation work.

semantic_distinctions.label: Dual-stack vs tunneling
semantic_distinctions.description: Dual-stack runs both stacks natively; tunneling encapsulates one protocol within another network.

semantic_distinctions.label: IPv4-mapped vs IPv4-compatible
semantic_distinctions.description: IPv4-mapped addresses remain a hybrid representation; IPv4-compatible addresses are deprecated.

semantic_distinctions.label: Stable vs temporary addresses
semantic_distinctions.description: Stable/global identifiers support reachability but can facilitate tracking; temporary addresses reduce persistence.

semantic_distinctions.label: AAAA vs A DNS records
semantic_distinctions.description: AAAA resolves IPv6; A resolves IPv4.

semantic_distinctions.label: PMTU discovery vs fragmentation
semantic_distinctions.description: PMTU discovery sizes packets for the path; fragmentation is endpoint-only when needed.

semantic_distinctions.label: IPsec vs higher-layer security
semantic_distinctions.description: The source discusses IPsec at the IP layer but does not equate it with TLS; both occupy different architectural positions.

semantic_distinctions.label: Native vs tunneled IPv6
semantic_distinctions.description: Native IPv6 traverses IPv6-capable infrastructure; tunneling carries IPv6 over IPv4 infrastructure.

misconceptions.title: IPv6 is just IPv4 with bigger addresses
misconceptions.correction: IPv6 changes packet format, address architecture, fragmentation behavior, neighbor discovery, multicast/broadcast semantics and other protocol functions.

misconceptions.title: IPv6 supports broadcast
misconceptions.correction: IPv6 does not define traditional broadcast addresses; multicast is used instead.

misconceptions.title: Routers fragment IPv6 packets
misconceptions.correction: IPv6 routers do not fragment; hosts use PMTU discovery or endpoint fragmentation.

misconceptions.title: IPv6 addresses always need DHCP
misconceptions.correction: IPv6 supports SLAAC and hosts generate link-local addresses automatically; DHCPv6 is optional for additional state.

misconceptions.title: Every IPv6 address is globally routable
misconceptions.correction: IPv6 interfaces require link-local addressing and may have multiple address types; global unicast is only one category.

misconceptions.title: IPv6 cannot be scanned
misconceptions.correction: The source explicitly notes that configuration patterns can make scanning feasible in real-world scenarios.

misconceptions.title: IPv6 has a header checksum like IPv4
IPv6 and IPv4 interoperate directly
misconceptions.correction: The source states the protocols are not directly interoperable and require transition mechanisms.

misconceptions.title: IPv6 extension headers are always harmless to routers
misconceptions.correction: Some implementations process extension headers in software/CPU paths, causing performance or security issues.

misconceptions.title: Global IPv6 addressing eliminates privacy concerns
misconceptions.correction: Stable globally addressable identifiers can facilitate tracking; temporary addresses mitigate this concern.

misconceptions.title: Tunneling is equivalent to native IPv6
misconceptions.correction: Tunneling adds encapsulation and can reduce MTU/increase latency.

misconceptions.title: NDP is just ARP with a new address format
misconceptions.correction: NDP uses ICMPv6 and multicast and also handles router discovery and address configuration.

misconceptions.title: AAAA records are IPv4 DNS records
misconceptions.correction: AAAA records map names to IPv6 addresses; A records map names to IPv4.

misconceptions.title: IPv6 deployment means IPv4 disappears immediately
misconceptions.correction: The source describes coexistence and transition mechanisms because both protocols operate simultaneously.

misconceptions.title: IPv6 security is automatically stronger because of the larger address space
misconceptions.correction: The source identifies implementation and operational security risks, including shadow networks and fragmentation evasion.

historical_context.label: Internet commercialization and growth
historical_context.description: Rapid Internet growth after commercialization made the IPv4 address supply problem apparent.

historical_context.label: Early-1990s IPng effort
historical_context.description: IETF began developing a next-generation IP protocol in response to projected Internet growth.

historical_context.label: 1993 IPng area
historical_context.description: IETF created a temporary ad hoc IP Next Generation area in September 1993.

historical_context.label: 1994 IPng model adoption
historical_context.description: IETF adopted the IPng model on 25 July 1994.

historical_context.label: 1998 IPv6 Draft Standard
historical_context.description: IPv6 became an IETF Draft Standard in December 1998.

historical_context.label: 2017 IPv6 Internet Standard
historical_context.description: IPv6 was ratified as an Internet Standard on 14 July 2017.

historical_context.label: 1999 IPv6 deployment beginning
historical_context.description: Source identifies July 1999 as the beginning of IPv6 deployment.

historical_context.label: Beijing 2008 IPv6 deployment
historical_context.description: IPv6 was used in a major world event at the Beijing 2008 Olympics.

historical_context.label: 2011 production OS support
historical_context.description: By 2011 major personal-computer and server operating systems had production-quality IPv6 implementations.
